questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I have always wanted to visit and live in Japan, so for me, it was an easy choice. The culture, food and living conditions are excellent as a student there.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
The host university gave online introductions and information briefs which helped immensely. In general, it was pretty easy to get the most important information.
Less "important" information (such as how to register for the gym, get transport discount) was more difficult to come by.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Online introductions by the host university, which helped with course registration. The RA at the dorm I lived in was also very helpful with everything from helping me register at the City Hall, to getting my student ID, etc. so I recommend living in a Waseda dorm!

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Very easy. The university sends out a questionnaire where you can apply for its three dorms, as well as its partner dorms/share houses. I would recommend applying for all three dorms and the partner ones that are close to campus. As far as I know, the vast majority got one of their choices. Very easy. The university sends out a questionnaire where you can apply for its three dorms, as well as its partner dorms/share houses. I would recommend applying for all three dorms and the partner ones that are close to campus. As far as I know, the vast majority got one of their choices.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: While it is "off-campus", all the dorms are extremely close to campus (a 5-minute walk). It made my experience much smoother since there were many people you could turn to for help with practical matters and similar. It also made it easy to make friends. But be prepared that you will not meet many Japanese people since the dorms are mostly international, so you have to seek them out. However, I can't think of a housing option where you will meet many Japanese people.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Some of the best friends I made while in Japan were from my dorm, and we did a lot of travelling and other fun activities in Tokyo. I would definitely recommend it as you often don't get the chance to meet students from other countries, and it is easy to find companions for trips/dinner/social things.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: It was very easy through their version of kunet.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There was an online introduction to course registraiton, a brief, and I could also write emails to them.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Attend the course registration guidance.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I took 5 courses. 1 was video on-demand, 2 were online on zoom and 2 were in person. The main reason why I do not give a higher score is the method of teaching. Zoom and video classes are, in my opinion, horrible and extremely demotivating to attend. The in-person classes were great, however.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The material is probably on the same level, maybe slightly lower, than in UCPH. However, the exams are much easier. In one course, I just had to do 4 30-minute quizzes during the semester, and that was it. In general, I spent probably 15-18 hours a week studying, which is a A LOT less than at UCPH.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The in-person classes were very small, maybe 8-10 people max. This made room for a lot of interaction with the teachers, which was great. There are no exercise classes, but the lectures feel like a mix of the two because of the high level of interaction. 

However, half my courses were on zoom. Anyone who has done classes on Zoom probably knows how boring it is, so I would not recommend taking these classes if you can avoid it.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Population Economics
Statistical Finance
Experimental Economics
Applied Microeconometrics
Market Design

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Experimental Economics was very interesting, and the teacher is fantastic. I would definitely recommend this course. 
Statistical Finance was interesting, and the quizzes mean you actually learn a lot. Even though it was on Zoom I did feel like the teacher made a good effort and I learned quite a bit. 
I would definitely recommend on taking the Japanese zero course (japanese language learning for people on level 0). I did not take it, and that is a big regret of mine.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: You have to enroll in Japanese health insurance. This is not very expensive, maybe 200 kr. per month, but I did not expect it.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Transport was less expensive than I thought. One thing to note is that all my transport fees were not actually university-related, since I could walk to uni in 5 minutes.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There are many, many student clubs and societies and I was impressed by the selection. However, it was difficult to get information on them and how to join, so I did not join any clubs. If you make the effort, I imagine it would be worth it, and it is probably the best way to meet Japanese people.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Many different ones. Some I looked at were a temple-outing club, a formula 1 club, and a karate club.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I did not really participate in any university-related non-academic activities.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I would definitely recommend taking day-trips out of Tokyo to the various mountains and hills that you can hike on, such as Mount Takao and Mount Mitake. It is also quite easy to take longer trips to other cities, such as Hiroshima, Kyoto, Nikko, and Kanazawa due to the bullet train. In general, Japan is a great place to explore and I would recommend you do this :)

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy, as I had been to Japan before. The most difficult thing is the language barrier. Not many speak good English, so you will have to get used to communicating with facial expressions, your hands and simple words. In the end, it wasn't that difficult and I quickly got used to it.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I imagine joining a club is the easiest way.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Again, the language barrier. I would definitely recommend getting a translator app (such as google translate). You will sometimes experience people that speak no English, or menu cards that are only in Japanese. In these situations, my translator app was crucial. Google maps was also very handy for transport (like rejseplanen).

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The politeness and service-level of the Japanese are incredible. I loved the food and I loved the temples and religious sites.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
-Take time to travel around.
-Live in a dorm
-Accept that you will not always know what is going on, that people will speak to you in a language you do not understand, but just go with the flow and everything will be fine :)

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Bring deodorant, it is impossible to find.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting new people and making friends all over the world. I would definitely recommend staying in an international dorm, for this reason. Other than that, I loved traveling around Japan, experiencing the amazing food, nature and cultural sites.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Language.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: I loved it, best 5 months ever.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
